U.S. District Judge David Carter, a Clinton appointee, denied DOJ's request for a temporary restraining order in a 26-page ruling issued Wednesday evening after a hearing in Los Angeles.

The Justice Department immediately filed a notice of appeal to the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals, with U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli saying he would seek an emergency order there; the case could eventually reach the U.S. Supreme Court.
California Attorney General Rob Bonta and Los Angeles County officials opposed the DOJ request, arguing the list is unreliable and that segregating ballots now would be unlawful and infeasible.
Court filings state more than 3.7 million ballots have already been cast in California, including over 500,000 processed this week after being separated from their identifying envelopes.

DOJ officials said the noncitizen list was built by comparing voter rolls to USCIS immigration, Social Security, and passport records, and that the department has charged dozens of people in the last two months for registering or voting as noncitizens.

USCIS official Nicolas Bartell said his office's review of a sampled subset found none were U.S.-born, though four 'might have a claim to U.S. citizenship'; expert witness Kassra Oskooi, retained by intervening voting rights groups, said USCIS's matching protocol 'is likely to be unreliable.'

Similar DOJ actions are underway elsewhere: a letter sent Monday to Washington state regarding 400 voters it believes are noncitizens, and a lawsuit filed last week in Alaska concerning certification of a Senate race.
ladder.analysis: This case sits at the intersection of federal authority and state control over election administration, a tension explicitly flagged by Judge Carter, who noted that states traditionally run their own elections and that no prior administration had attempted this kind of eve-of-election intervention. Both outlets confirm the judge's central reasoning rested on the practical and constitutional risks of disrupting an ongoing election rather than a definitive resolution of whether noncitizens are in fact on the rolls — that underlying factual dispute, including competing expert assessments of USCIS's data-matching process, remains unresolved and contested.

stories.headline: Russian drone attack on Dnipro train station kills at least 14
stories.byline: International & World desk · anchored on Reuters
body: At least 14 people were killed and 14 others wounded, including an 11-year-old boy, when a Russian jet-powered drone struck the main railway station in the central Ukrainian city of Dnipro on Thursday, local officials said. The attack hit a crowded platform where a passenger train headed for Zaporizhzhia and a commuter train were standing, according to Ukrzaliznytsia, Ukraine's state railway operator. Dnipropetrovsk regional head Oleksandr Hanzha confirmed the death toll and injuries.

Ukrzaliznytsia head Oleksandr Pertsovsky said an elevated threat level had been announced ahead of the strike, 'but unfortunately there were still a large number of people on the platform' when the drone hit. Dnipro Mayor Borys Filatov called the incident a tragedy, adding that a drone hit a civilian electric train. Photographs from rescue services showed a large hole in the platform near a blast-damaged train with smashed windows.

The Dnipro attack came as other Russian strikes hit Ukraine on Thursday. In the northern city of Chernihiv, two 15-year-old girls were killed and at least 25 others, including four children, injured in a missile strike, according to regional head Vyacheslav Chaus. In Kremenchuk, Poltava region, three people were killed and 28 injured in a drone attack that hit residential buildings and a school, regional head Vitaliy Diakivnych said. Chernihiv announced a day of mourning for Friday.

The attacks occurred during a fragile local ceasefire in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, brokered by U.S. first lady Melania Trump. Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said the truce was holding into its third day and that he had set out with a Ukrainian delegation toward Oleshky via Belarus and Russia. The ceasefire is set to last until 10:59 p.m. local time on November 1. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky condemned the Dnipro strike as 'horrific' and called for tougher sanctions from the U.S., EU, and G7, criticizing a recent deal between Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin that eased sanctions on Russian diesel imports. Ukrainian sanctions commissioner Vladyslav Vlasiuk told CNN: 'You cannot lift sanctions and then expect the Russians to take any action. Constructive actions must come first, and then everything else.'

Meanwhile, the Kremlin condemned Ukrainian drone attacks on Moscow during the Russia-Africa Summit, according to Tass. Moscow's mayor said 613 Ukrainian drones were launched overnight toward the region, most of which were shot down. Russia's defense ministry has denied deliberately targeting civilians, saying its strikes target infrastructure used to transport military personnel and equipment. However, data from Ukrzaliznytsia show attacks on railway facilities have risen sharply: of 521 locomotives hit since the start of the full-scale invasion in February 2022, almost 60% have been struck this year, with overall attacks on railway facilities rising from 1,206 in 2025 to 1,700 so far this year.

stories.headline: Audio recordings show control room errors before deadly Spain train crash; at least 68 dead
body: Audio recordings released by Spanish media reveal that a railway control center gave a high-speed train clearance to proceed at normal speed moments before it slammed into a stationary train in central Spain on Wednesday, killing at least 68 people and injuring about 80 others, 15 critically. The crash, which occurred near Urda in the Toledo province, involved a state-owned Renfe train carrying 397 passengers and a private Iryo train with 147 passengers that had stalled ahead on the same line after losing communication with the automatic signaling system.

In the recordings published by outlets including El País and RTVE, a control operator tells the Renfe driver to continue under a backup system called Lateral Signalling Block 'at normal speed with normal operation.' When the driver asks for confirmation—'At normal speed?'—the controller replies, 'Yes.' Earlier exchanges show that the Iryo driver had notified the control center that the train was stationary and could not be restarted because the security system prevented it. Spain's transport minister, Óscar Puente, called the decision to order movement without speed restrictions 'inexplicable.'

The crash is Spain's second deadly high-speed rail disaster this year, following a January collision that killed 46 people. Until 2024, the country's high-speed network—the second largest in the world after China's—had not suffered a fatal accident in over three decades. Spain only liberalized its high-speed service in 2021, with the Italian operator Iryo beginning operations the following year. The Spanish Union of Railway Drivers (Semaf) proceeded with a planned strike on Thursday, citing concerns over railway safety.

Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, who visited the crash site, declared three days of national mourning and vowed a thorough investigation. 'It is not acceptable for a country like Spain to endure two high-speed train accidents in the same year,' he said. The disaster comes less than a month before a snap national election scheduled for November 29. Most political parties cancelled their campaigns, but the far-right Vox party continued, with leader Santiago Abascal accusing rivals of trying to 'use mourning to silence criticism' of infrastructure. Opposition leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo said 'Spain has the right to know what is happening with its infrastructure.'

Among the victims was 24-year-old long jumper Julieta Gallego, who competed for Madrid-based club AD Sprint. The Royal Spanish Athletics Federation confirmed her death, with federation president Raúl Chapado saying, 'There are blows that strike at the very heart of the athletics family.' Emergency crews deployed more than 900 personnel from the Civil Guard, using drones and helicopters to search the wreckage. Survivors described scenes of smoke, fire, and trapped passengers. Late Wednesday, about 1,500 protesters gathered outside the Transport Ministry in Madrid, demanding the resignations of Sánchez and Puente; police used tear gas after some threw bottles and flares.

stories.headline: Netanyahu's bloc leads Israel election but falls short of majority
body: Partial results from Israel's general election show Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's right-wing bloc leading but falling short of a majority in the 120-seat Knesset. With 99% of ballots counted, Netanyahu's Likud party and its far-right and ultra-Orthodox Jewish allies were on track to win 53 seats, while former military chief Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party and three other Jewish opposition parties in his bloc were set for 48. Arab-led parties, on course to win an unprecedented 19 seats, could emerge as kingmakers, but all but one of the Jewish parties have pledged not to work with them.

Tuesday's election was the first since the deadly Hamas-led attacks on Israel on 7 October 2023 and the subsequent wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran. Key campaign issues included accountability for the security failures that led to the attacks, the conduct of regional wars, conscripting ultra-Orthodox Jewish men into the military, judicial reforms, and Israel's international standing. Turnout was 77.7%, the highest in more than two decades, which President Isaac Herzog called 'a badge of honour for Israeli society.'

Both Netanyahu and Eisenkot have insisted they should be tasked with forming a governing coalition. Netanyahu declared his right-wing bloc had won a 'great majority' and said it was 'forbidden to endanger Israel by forming a government that relies on anti-Zionist Arab parties.' Eisenkot told supporters that 'the coalition of failure has lost the people's trust' and that he would work to ensure 'the people's decision is translated into a Zionist government.'

The two Arab parties — the United Arab List and the Joint List — are set to almost double their representation due to a surge in turnout among Arab Israelis, who account for about a fifth of the population. Joint List head Yousef Jabareen said Arab voters were motivated in part by the opportunity to remove far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, whom he accused of racism. United Arab List leader Mansour Abbas expressed hope that his party, the Change Bloc, and the UAL could secure 61 Knesset seats. However, Eisenkot has previously raised objections to such an alliance, including conditions that Arab parties recognise Israel as Jewish and democratic.

Netanyahu's Likud party has accused the Arab parties of 'stealing' the election, filing a complaint with the Central Elections Committee (CEC) alleging 'bribery, threats, violence, fraud and the use of prohibited software to encourage voters' without providing evidence. On Thursday, CEC chairman Justice Noam Sohlberg instructed the Shin Bet domestic security service to investigate 'serious suspicions' regarding 'improper influence through foreign funding by external actors operating against Israeli interests.' The Haaretz newspaper cited a source saying the committee had been presented with a claim that Qatar had provided funding aimed at increasing voter turnout in Arab communities. Likud called it 'an attack on democracy aimed at enabling foreign control of the Knesset.' Balad chairman Sami Abu Shehadeh dismissed the allegation as a 'racist blood libel.'

Qatar's Foreign Ministry spokesman Majed al-Ansari denied the allegations, calling them 'ridiculous and dangerous in equal measure' and part of a 'disinformation campaign.' He said Qatar has 'no involvement' in Israel's political or electoral competition. Dean Livine, acting director for Israel's CEC, rejected allegations of foreign interference, stating that 'the Knesset elections were conducted lawfully.' Once results are confirmed, President Herzog will hold consultations with all factions and invite the leader he believes has the best chance to form a government, a process that could take weeks. If no coalition is formed, another election would be required.

stories.headline: Aid mission set to enter Oleshky as localized Russia-Ukraine truce holds for third day
body: Humanitarian aid is poised to roll into the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in Ukraine's Kherson region on Friday, a Ukrainian official said, as a localized ceasefire between Moscow and Kyiv stretched into a third day. The truce, which took effect on October 27, has held for 54 hours as of Thursday, with both sides reporting no violations. Military engineers have been clearing landmines from roads to prepare a safe passage for the humanitarian convoy, which is expected to deliver food and medical supplies to about 2,000 residents still trapped in the devastated city.

The ceasefire was brokered with the involvement of U.S. first lady Melania Trump, whom both sides thanked for her role, and was also pressed for by Pope Leo XIV. Ukrainian ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets confirmed the truce was holding and that aid deliveries were due to begin Friday, while his Russian counterpart, Yana Lantratova, said Russian engineers were working on de-mining roads in Oleshky. Lantratova stated she was on her way to Oleshky for the aid delivery, and Lubinets arrived in Belarus en route to the city, as part of an operation that Lantratova said was five months in the making.

Preparations for the evacuation of civilians are also underway, according to Myroslava Kharchenko, a lawyer with the Save Ukraine Foundation. She told DW that registration lists are being circulated through closed local chat groups, with organizers collecting information on residents' health conditions, including those who are ill, have limited mobility, or are recovering from blast and mine-related wounds. Kharchenko estimated that around 500 people may eventually be evacuated, though she noted that many residents remain fearful due to previous failed attempts to establish humanitarian corridors. The evacuation route is expected to pass through temporarily occupied Ukrainian territory and possibly Russia, but details are being kept confidential for security reasons.

The truce has brought a rare and welcome stillness to the nearby Ukrainian-held city of Kherson, which has also been wracked by the war. Nataliia Myronenko, 42, who runs a coffee kiosk, said she had a steady stream of customers since the quiet began. "It's a breath of freedom, when you don't look at the sky. You keep looking at your feet because of the mines, but you're not afraid of dying," she said, adding, "It's such a privilege and a joy, but we understand it will end soon."

Despite the localized truce, the broader war continued elsewhere. A Russian drone strike hit two trains stopped at a station in Dnipro, central Ukraine, killing at least 13 people and injuring 10 others, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who called it a "horrific attack." Russia's Defense Ministry said air defenses downed 1,214 Ukrainian drones overnight in one of the largest drone attacks launched by Kyiv, with around half heading toward Moscow, according to Mayor Sergei Sobyanin.

The temporary ceasefire comes amid shifting diplomatic dynamics. Moscow and Kyiv are both keen to curry favor with Washington ahead of possible three-way talks next month between Russia, Ukraine, and the United States. U.S. President Donald Trump has recently indicated disengagement with Kyiv, waiving sanctions on Russia and publicly chiding Zelenskyy, while Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov is set to travel to the U.S. for a G20 ministerial meeting in Atlanta starting Friday. Meanwhile, Russian President Vladimir Putin praised Elon Musk as "a genius" and said Russia has been in contact with the tech billionaire to coordinate satellite activities, as Ukraine earlier this month reported unexpected limits on Starshield, the military-grade Starlink service that is critical to its drone operations and communications.

stories.headline: Middle East braces for possible Iran war escalation amid diplomatic efforts
body: Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey sent senior envoys to Tehran on Monday for direct talks aimed at preventing a new military escalation, as the United States warned Middle Eastern allies to prepare for a possible short, intense renewal of the war with Iran after the US midterm election on November 3. Pakistan's army chief Asim Munir, Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin—representing the newly formed Mecca defense pact—met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and other senior officials. The trip was officially intended to open negotiating channels and "prevent the return of military escalation," according to Saudi Arabia.

Iran described the atmosphere as "very positive" and said "very good discussions" took place, though no breakthroughs were announced. Mohsen Rezaei, head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, told state television: "I feel that a new atmosphere is emerging in the region." However, Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei later called for protecting Iran's interests and maintaining Tehran's conditions for ending both the war and the current state of "neither war nor peace." A senior Pakistani official said the talks focused on building a regional non-aggression network, US-Iran negotiations, Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, the Strait of Hormuz, and the US naval blockade. Another official said Munir presented a solution that would offer something to both Washington and Iran, with the three Mecca states and Qatar as mediators, and that US President Donald Trump had previously given Munir the go-ahead for diplomacy.

The united front by the three nations signals the growing coordination of the Mecca defense alliance, established this summer, under which an attack on one member is considered an attack on all. Saudi Arabia, Iran's longtime regional rival, faces mounting costs from Houthi attacks on its infrastructure—launched by the Iran-aligned group—but also fears a wider war could threaten its investment-driven economic strategy. Egypt's parliament agreed on the same day to give military help to Riyadh and take "all necessary measures" to help Saudi Arabia defend itself. Analysts noted the Mecca pact is designed primarily for deterrence, but its members could shift from mediation to a different posture if escalation continues.

Alongside the Tehran talks, Iran pursued other diplomatic channels. President Pezeshkian traveled to Moscow for the Gas Exporting Countries Forum, where he met Russian President Vladimir Putin and Qatar's Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, discussing the war and the Strait of Hormuz. Meanwhile, US Vice President Vance made outreach to Tehran, and the US told Gulf allies to "be ready" for possible renewed action. Iran's media adviser Ali Asghar Shafieian rejected the notion that the Mecca envoys presented an ultimatum, saying that like the US and Israel, Iran can strengthen its military capabilities while maintaining negotiations. An agreement remains possible, he said, if Iran's political standing and national dignity are respected.

The diplomatic push comes as the US has privately warned Gulf states of a possible short, intense resumption of the war after the November 3 midterm elections. Iran has not publicly offered guarantees over Houthi attacks—a key Saudi demand—and analysts say Tehran is following a strategy of extending negotiations while avoiding firm commitments. The Houthi rebels remain central to Iran's leverage. The only apparent outcome of the Monday meeting is a commitment to keep talking, which for Iran signals that it remains a diplomatic partner rather than a target. The risk of a broader conflict persists, with no deal announced and both sides preparing for the possibility of renewed fighting.

stories.headline: U.S. GDP grows 3.4% in Q3, inflation accelerates with PCE at 3.6%
body: The U.S. economy expanded at a faster-than-expected annualized pace of 3.4% in the third quarter, the Commerce Department reported Thursday, while the Federal Reserve’s preferred inflation gauge accelerated in September, signaling that the central bank’s fight against rising prices is far from over.

Gross domestic product grew at a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.4%, beating the 3.1% estimate and accelerating from 2.2% in the second quarter. The personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index rose 0.5% in September from August, the largest monthly increase since March, pushing the annual inflation rate to 3.6%. Excluding food and energy, core PCE rose 0.3% month over month and 3.1% year over year. Both the headline and core monthly readings were in line with consensus estimates.

The data come one day after the Federal Reserve voted to hold its benchmark interest rate in a range of 3.75%–4%. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said Wednesday that policymakers are not on a preset path, noting, “If we had a firm conclusion about the conduct of monetary policy, we'd announce it to much fanfare today.” However, Thursday’s reports show inflation remains well above the Fed’s 2% target, and markets are now pricing in an 83% chance of a quarter-point rate hike in December, according to the CME FedWatch tool.

September’s PCE increase was driven largely by a 9.2% jump in gasoline and other energy goods, with energy goods and services broadly rising 5.4%. Services prices excluding energy and housing rose 0.4%, and housing costs increased 0.3%. Despite the inflation pressure, consumer spending remained resilient, climbing 0.5% in September — slightly below the 0.6% forecast — while personal income rose 0.2%, missing the 0.3% estimate.

Third-quarter growth was supported by robust consumer spending, which rose 3.8%, and a surge in investment. Gross private domestic investment soared 19.4%, led by a 20.9% increase in equipment spending and an 8.4% rise in intellectual property products. A separate Labor Department report showed initial jobless claims fell to 194,000 for the week ended October 24, below the 200,000 estimate and near late-1960s lows, indicating a still-tight labor market.

Following the releases, stock market futures turned negative and Treasury yields fell. The 10-year yield hovered near 4.97%, while the 2-year yield traded at 4.635%. “Net, net, economic growth is powering ahead despite the uncertainty of geopolitical risks and the damage posed to many sectors of the economy by higher energy costs,” said Chris Rupkey, chief economist at Fwdbonds. Stephen Coltman, head of macro at 21shares, noted that Fed Chair Warsh sees the economy as strong and inflation above target, and that today’s data will not change that assessment, meaning investors should expect the Fed funds rate to continue to rise.

stories.headline: Alphabet plunges 13%, heads for record $500B value loss on AI-driven miss
body: Alphabet shares plunged about 13% in early trading Thursday, putting the Google parent on track for its worst single-day loss since going public in 2004 and threatening to erase nearly $500 billion in market value. The sell-off follows a third-quarter earnings report that missed analyst estimates on search revenue and revealed a deeper-than-expected swing to negative free cash flow, raising fresh concerns that artificial intelligence services are beginning to cannibalize Google’s core search business.

Alphabet reported earnings per share of $2.12 on revenue of $127.58 billion, compared with analyst expectations of $3.01 and $127.93 billion, respectively. Revenue excluding traffic acquisition costs came in at $111.21 billion, slightly below the $111.29 billion estimate. Search and other advertising revenue grew 12% year over year to about $63 billion, falling short of the roughly $65 billion Wall Street had forecast. Google Cloud revenue more than doubled to about $31 billion, exceeding the $29.1 billion estimate, and Alphabet said its Gemini app passed 1 billion users. However, free cash flow swung to a loss of about $9.07 billion in the quarter, three times the $2.70 billion deficit analysts had anticipated, as spending on AI data centers and infrastructure climbed.

The gap between search query growth—which Alphabet said was the strongest in five years—and decelerating search revenue has sharpened investor anxiety. In the first quarter, search revenue grew 19%; it slid to 17% in the second quarter and then to 12% in the third. “The bears will argue this is the first quarter that AI is starting to seriously hurt their search business,” said Jeffrey Wlodarczak, CEO of Pivotal Research. Alphabet’s chief business officer, Philipp Schindler, attributed part of the miss to lower monetization within the company’s AI Mode and said Google is scaling ads in AI Overviews and AI Mode products internationally. Despite the pullback, CFRA analyst Angelo Zino called the decline “probably a buying opportunity.”

Alphabet maintained its full-year capital expenditure guidance of between $195 billion and $205 billion and said spending will increase significantly in 2027, as it invests in tensor processing units and data centers to meet cloud and AI demand. The cloud backlog reached roughly $560 billion, reflecting contracted demand for AI infrastructure, with management expecting just over half to be recognized over the next 24 months. CFO Anat Ashkenazi noted that cash is going out to build inventory and will come in as systems are delivered. The company’s stakes in AI labs also contributed to the free-cash-flow shortfall.

The losses underscore the market’s heightened sensitivity to AI spending and search trends. Alphabet’s previous worst one-day market-value decline was about $275 billion on July 23; the $500 billion drop would be the second largest ever for a U.S.-listed company, trailing only Nvidia’s $593 billion loss on Jan. 27, 2025, after China’s DeepSeek rattled AI investors. US-listed stocks have shed $200 billion or more in a single session 18 times so far this year, up from 13 in all of 2025 and none before 2022. Alphabet alone has lost about $1.4 trillion since its record in May.

Microsoft, which reported earnings Wednesday, saw its shares trade largely flat as its free cash flow remained positive at $18.63 billion despite a 27% decline, and capital expenditures of $45.2 billion came in below analyst projections. “Alphabet, by contrast, saw its share price hit after hours as a result of a fairly messy set of results and a poorly handled earnings call,” said Ben Barringer of Quilter Cheviot. Investors now await Amazon’s quarterly report after Thursday’s close; faster growth at Amazon Web Services without a hit to cash flow would point to a problem specific to Google’s search business, while another quarter of cash burn would keep pressure on the broader AI spending narrative.

stories.headline: Brewers clinch World Series title; Milwaukee-area businesses offer free food and drink
body: The Milwaukee Brewers defeated the Tampa Bay Rays 4-1 in Game 5 of the World Series on Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026, at Tropicana Field in St. Petersburg, Florida, clinching the championship. After the final out, the team celebrated in the clubhouse with the Commissioner's Trophy, with players including Jackson Chourio, Jacob Misiorowski, Cooper Pratt, Brandon Woodruff, Sal Frelick, Christian Yelich and Chad Patrick joining the festivities.

Milwaukee took control in the second inning, when Brice Turang doubled off Rays starter Drew Rasmussen and Sal Frelick was hit by a pitch. Tampa Bay third baseman Junior Caminero singled off Brewers pitcher Jacob Misiorowski, who worked the early innings at Tropicana Field, where empty seats were visible during the first inning. The Rays never got closer, and the Brewers closed out the 4-1 victory to end the series.

Back in Wisconsin, Milwaukee-area businesses are joining the celebration. Milwaukee Brat House, at 1013 N. King Drive, promised free bratwursts before the clincher and plans to make good on that offer, though details have not yet been shared. Georgie Porgie's, the fast-casual diner in Oak Creek and Racine, is giving away free junior-size Brew Moon shakes all day Thursday, Oct. 29, while supplies last, with no purchase necessary. Brew Moon is the Brewers' postseason special: blue moon frozen custard topped with whipped cream and blue and yellow sprinkles.

Tally's Tap & Eatery at S31W24661 W. Sunset Drive in Waukesha will host a Free Beer Day on Monday, Nov. 2, offering free Miller Lite draft beer starting at noon while supplies last, fulfilling the promise on its exterior sign: "If the Brewers win it all, free beer for y'all." Thursday is Victory Thursday in Milwaukee, where fans marked the title at an American Family Field watch party during Game 5, and more deals could still be coming.

stories.headline: Bears acquire All-Pro DT Jeffery Simmons in blockbuster trade with Titans
body: The Chicago Bears acquired four-time Pro Bowl defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons from the Tennessee Titans, sending first-round picks in 2027 and 2028 along with a 2027 fourth-round pick to Tennessee in exchange for Simmons and a 2028 fifth-round pick, according to multiple reports. The deal marks the biggest pre-deadline trade this season and significantly alters the trajectory of both franchises.

Simmons, 29, is coming off a first-team All-Pro season in 2025 and signed a three-year, $105.8 million extension with the Titans this offseason. He has played 86.7% of Tennessee's defensive snaps this season (425 of 490), ranking among the highest usage rates for an interior lineman. Known as a high-motor pass rusher and elite run stopper who draws frequent double teams, Simmons recorded seven pressures in a Week 6 game against the Colts despite facing multiple blockers. He instantly becomes the Bears' best defensive player, according to Yahoo Sports, and is expected to start immediately alongside Grady Jarrett on the interior.

The Bears have been aggressive in upgrading their talent ahead of the deadline after previously expressing interest in Colts defensive tackle DeForest Buckner before he was traded to San Francisco. Chicago's defense ranks eighth in yards allowed and 10th in points allowed but is near the bottom in several per-play metrics, buoyed by an offense that leads the league in time of possession (35:30 per game). The team faces a brutal remaining schedule, including two games against the Lions and matchups with the Jaguars and Bills. The addition of Simmons, combined with the return of pass rusher Montez Sweat from suspension and the eventual returns of Shemar Turner and Dayo Odeyingbo, could transform a below-average defensive line into a strength.

For the Titans, the trade continues a full-scale rebuild under first-year general manager Mike Borgonzi. Tennessee is 1-6 and holds the No. 2 overall pick in the upcoming draft. By acquiring two future first-rounders along with a fourth-round pick, the Titans now have six selections in the first four rounds of the 2027 draft and significant flexibility for 2028. Yahoo Sports notes the deal gives the Titans protection if quarterback Cam Ward, the No. 1 overall pick in 2025, does not develop as hoped. Borgonzi likely had multiple bidders for Simmons and was able to extract a premium price, including a fourth-round pick in 2027 for a 2028 fifth-round sweetener.

History offers mixed results for teams that stockpile multiple first-round picks, as CBS Sports notes. The Chiefs (2022), Eagles (2023) and Seahawks (2023) all used multiple first-round selections to build Super Bowl winners, while the Jets used three first-rounders in 2022 on Sauce Gardner, Garrett Wilson and Jermaine Johnson—each earning individual accolades—yet never made the playoffs and saw two of those players traded within four years. The Browns similarly had five first-round picks in 2017 and 2018, won one playoff game, but failed to sustain success. The Titans will need to pair their draft capital with sound quarterback play and roster construction to avoid a similar fate.

Yahoo Sports graded the trade a B for the Bears, noting the steep cost of two first-round picks but that the move could prove smart if Chicago makes a Super Bowl run. The Titans received an A-minus, reflecting strong value for an elite player on a team facing a multi-year rebuild. Simmons is under contract for 3.5 more seasons after signing his extension, giving the Bears a premier interior presence in his prime as they push for a championship.

stories.headline: HHS temporarily allows compounding pharmacies to produce six unapproved peptides
body: The Department of Health and Human Services has issued a policy that will temporarily allow state-licensed compounding pharmacies, federal facilities, and licensed physicians to manufacture six unapproved peptides — BPC-157, Epitalon, KPV, MOTS-c, Semax, and TB-500 — without facing federal enforcement. The policy, announced by Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., uses what the department called "enforcement discretion" and comes despite objections from career scientists at the Food and Drug Administration who said there is scant evidence the substances are safe or effective. Kennedy, who has been a vocal supporter of peptides and has said he has used some himself, filed the draft policy on Wednesday.

Peptides are strings of amino acids shorter than proteins that can exert powerful effects in the body; some occur naturally and others are synthetic variations. The six covered substances are not FDA-approved but are widely promoted by wellness influencers and some clinicians for a range of unproven uses: BPC-157 for ulcerative colitis, Epitalon for insomnia, KPV for wound healing, MOTS-c for metabolic health, Semax for migraine, and TB-500 for wound healing. BPC-157 and TB-500 have also become popular as an injury-recovery duo. The policy does not grant FDA approval or establish clinical safety and effectiveness, an HHS spokesperson said. Kennedy cited a July recommendation from an FDA advisory committee, saying the policy "advances patient choice and freedom while appropriately protecting patient safety." The HHS spokesperson said the policy requires patient-specific prescriptions, traceable ingredients, quality testing, and safety reporting, including an FDA-registered ingredient maker, a lab certificate for raw ingredients, and reports of serious side effects — holding compounders accountable and giving patients "an alternative to unregulated sellers."

The peptides have been available online as "research-use-only" products, often sourced from sketchy overseas suppliers, despite an official ban. In July, an FDA advisory panel voted to recommend that compounding pharmacies be cleared to make the six substances, but at the same meeting the FDA's own scientists recommended against unwinding existing restrictions, saying there is not enough evidence of safety and effectiveness for each peptide. The new policy applies only to smaller "503A" compounding pharmacies, not the larger "503B" outsourcing facilities that produce higher volumes of medicines. It does not change the peptides' legal status, but creates a path for small compounders to produce them in limited quantities.

Industry reaction highlighted both opportunity and likely supply constraints. Joshua Fritzler, president of Olympia and Wesley Pharmaceuticals in central Florida, said people have asked about these peptides for years but his company did not make them because they were illegal to compound. Now only his smaller facility will be able to make them, in small quantities. "We won't be able to meet demand," he said, adding that Olympia will likely compound only one of the six peptides and needs to prepare its facility first. "I don't think all the [503]As in the country could meet the demand." Scott Brunner, CEO of the Alliance for Pharmacy Compounding, said his group is pleased because the policy offers a "more accountable alternative" for patients seeking gray market peptides and "brings patients into a system where pharmacy standards, regulatory oversight, and serious adverse event reporting apply." He warned, however, that it may take time for pharmacies to begin dispensing because ingredient suppliers must ensure their active ingredients meet the policy's requirements, and pharmacies must verify that too.

Consumer advocacy groups sharply criticized the move. Public Citizen's Dr. Robert Steinbrook, director of the Health Research Group, said Kennedy acted unilaterally rather than through the typical rulemaking process. "By allowing unproven and potentially unsafe peptides to be manufactured, marketed and prescribed without concern about potential federal enforcement actions, Kennedy has undermined the FDA and threatened public health," Steinbrook said in a statement. He argued that all peptide substances should go through the standard FDA approval process for new drugs and that the HHS Secretary should "support, not sabotage" FDA enforcement actions, while advising clinicians to warn patients about the risk of contamination and other adverse effects. The Partnership for Safe Medicines, which includes various pharmacy and pharmacist organizations, filed a citizen petition last week urging the FDA to ignore its advisory committee's July recommendation. Executive director Shabbir Safda said, "Today's decision leaves Americans in a grey area as to whether peptides are safe or not, even though the FDA's own scientists recommended against voting in favor of these substances due to concerns with evidence."

The policy, which the department said it intends to use enforcement discretion rather than take action against licensed pharmacies and physicians compounding the six peptides, comes as the FDA continues to weigh whether to allow compounding pharmacies to manufacture them. The measures are temporary and do not constitute approval, meaning patients seeking these products may still face limited availability while pharmacies verify ingredients and prepare their facilities. The move was framed by the administration as expanding access to experimental wellness therapies embraced by many in the Make America Healthy Again movement, but critics say it undermines the FDA's drug review process and leaves patients without evidence of safety or effectiveness.

stories.headline: Apple launches touchscreen MacBook Pro with OLED display starting at $2,899
body: Apple today announced a touchscreen MacBook Pro with an OLED display, marking the company's first major redesign of the laptop in more than five years and ending a long-standing resistance to touch input on macOS. The new MacBook Pro is available in 14-inch and 16-inch sizes, powered by M5 Pro or M5 Max chips, with up to 128GB of unified memory and up to 16TB of storage. Preorders open October 30, with availability beginning November 6.

The display, branded as PROLED XDR, achieves 2,000 nits peak brightness for HDR and SDR, a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio, and retains a 120 Hz variable refresh rate. Apple redesigned the hinge to stabilize the screen and reduce wobble, though demos showed some movement remains. The 14-inch model weighs just 3 pounds, about half a pound lighter than its predecessor. A Dynamic Island cutout replaces the previous notch, and the Apple logo on the back now glows again.

Pricing starts at $2,899 for the base configuration, nearly $1,000 more than the regular MacBook Pro. The fully loaded 16-inch model reaches $14,549, up $4,400 from the previous generation's top-tier price of $10,149. Upgrades include a 16TB SSD for an additional $7,000, 128GB of memory for $2,000, and nano-texture glass for $150.

Apple had long resisted a touchscreen Mac. In 2010, Steve Jobs called such laptops “ergonomically terrible.” Tim Cook later described hybrid designs as a compromise, saying “you can converge a toaster and a refrigerator, but those things are probably not going to be pleasing to the user.” Craig Federighi in 2014 called the Mac a “sit-down experience” and said a touchscreen was “not the right interface.” However, Apple marketing chief Greg Joswiak acknowledged the shift, telling Wired: “There’s a generation of young creators and young people using our MacBook Pros that expect to touch.” Apple CEO John Ternus added, “You’ve gotta touch it to believe it.”

Apple has adapted macOS for touch, redesigning the menu bar to allow easier selection and enlarging window-control buttons when touched. The Dynamic Island can be tapped for quick controls, and gestures such as swiping between spaces, accessing Mission Control, and pinch-to-zoom are supported. The company is relying on developers to support touch in their apps, though basic functions like scrolling and zooming work out of the box. This approach contrasts with the Touch Bar, a touchscreen strip introduced in 2016 that failed due to inconsistent app support and was removed in 2023.

The launch validates years of effort by Microsoft to bring touch to laptops, with Windows incorporating multitouch support since Windows 7 and the Surface Pro line demonstrating the utility of touch on a PC. Apple’s decision raises questions about future convergence of macOS, iOS, and iPadOS. The new MacBook Pro does not feature a convertible design; users reach up to touch the screen in a traditional clamshell configuration.

stories.headline: DoorDash to acquire Instacart for $17 billion
body: DoorDash announced Thursday it has agreed to acquire Instacart for approximately $17 billion, combining two major players in on-demand delivery. The deal, valued at $65 per Instacart share, has been approved by both companies’ boards and is expected to close near the end of 2027 or in the first half of 2028, subject to regulatory approvals.

The acquisition will give DoorDash a larger foothold in online grocery delivery by adding Instacart’s established grocery marketplace and retailer partnerships. “Grocery is one of the hardest things to get right online,” said DoorDash CEO Tony Xu in a statement. “Someone has to pick a ripe avocado, find a substitute you’d choose yourself, and get the ice cream to you before it melts. Instacart has spent years learning to do that well for grocers, while DoorDash has built a delivery network and technology that local stores rely on every day. Together, we could give stores of every size more of those tools and unlock the potential of grocery delivery.”

Instacart CEO Chris Rogers said the deal will “make online grocery more seamless and affordable” for millions of households, and that “joining forces with DoorDash allows us to do even more.” DoorDash plans to preserve Instacart’s brand, enterprise technology products, and app, meaning the two services will remain separate rather than merging into a single platform. The company said local grocers will not face platform exclusivity requirements, and Instacart shoppers will retain flexibility over their hours and orders, with the option to accept DoorDash orders or continue only with Instacart.

The deal comes amid increasing competition in the delivery market. DoorDash, which began as a restaurant courier, already operates its own grocery delivery business but faces rivals including Amazon, Walmart, and Uber. Uber has expanded into food delivery through acquisitions of Postmates and Delivery Hero. Rumors of a potential Instacart sale surfaced last week, with reports that Instacart had been in talks with Uber before discussions ended. By Monday, The Wall Street Journal reported DoorDash was in “advanced talks,” and the deal was confirmed Thursday.

DoorDash said the combination will give Instacart users access to more than 50,000 additional stores and allow DashPass and Instacart Plus members to pay a single membership fee instead of two. The company also noted that the deal could help grocers build their own online ordering and advertising businesses using Instacart’s technology, while taking advantage of DoorDash’s fulfillment services to offer lower-cost delivery. TechCrunch reported that Instacart, which has a market cap of more than $13 billion and a stock price up 25% year to date, may have viewed this as an opportune time to sell ahead of intensifying competition.

The acquisition is subject to regulatory review and other closing conditions. DoorDash said that until the transaction closes, the two companies will continue to operate independently. Both CEOs expressed optimism that the combined company can better serve local stores and consumers in the growing online grocery market.
